sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
This is the largest topic. It follows water from rain, across the land, through channels, pipes and pumps, into the ground, and through treatment before and after people use it.

Split it into three parts when studying: how much water there is (hydrology), how it moves (hydraulics) and how it is cleaned (treatment).
pitfalls: Using the wrong form of Manning's equation: the SI form has no 1.49 factor.
Giving detention time in days when the options are in hours.

tips.from: Mark Mattson, FE Water Resources Engineering Review Session 2022
items: In the rational formula, inches per hour times acres gives cubic feet per second directly. The units look wrong, but the handbook formula is set up that way.
Know what initial abstraction covers in the NRCS method, since concept questions ask about it: the losses before runoff starts.
In Manning's equation the hydraulic radius is raised to the 2/3 power. Put the exponent in parentheses on the calculator.
To turn a pressure into a head, divide by the specific weight in matching units: 62.4 lb/ft^{3} goes with pounds per square foot.
When a formula needs a height or a head, check which one: usually a difference between two levels.
Ultimate BOD from a five-day value: divide BOD_{5} by (1 - e^{-k t}).
Hardness, softening and flow regime (Froude number) are worth knowing; recent examinees reported them.

sections.title: Basic hydrology
sections.body:
Hydrology follows rain from the sky to the stream. Some rain is caught by plants, some soaks in (infiltration), and the rest runs off. The share that runs off depends on the surface: pavement sheds nearly all of it, and forest very little.

The rational method estimates the peak flow from a small catchment using a runoff coefficient, the rainfall intensity for a storm lasting as long as the time of concentration, and the area. The NRCS curve number method estimates the depth of runoff from a storm. A hydrograph plots flow against time.
pitfalls: Using a rainfall intensity for the wrong storm duration. It should match the time of concentration.

example.problem: A 5 acre site with C = 0.4 receives rain at 3 in/h. Find the peak runoff.

ideas.title: Time of concentration
ideas.text: It is the time for runoff from the farthest part of the catchment to reach the outlet, after which the whole area is contributing: overland flow time plus travel time in gutters and sewers. Rain starts everywhere at once, so with several sub-areas use the longest path, not the sum.

ideas.title: Composite curve number
ideas.text: Where land covers are mixed, use the area-weighted average curve number. Pavement is assigned 98, not 100, because surface pits hold a little water.

ideas.title: Runoff is a depth
ideas.text: The NRCS method gives runoff in inches over the catchment. Rainfall minus runoff is what the site kept. Initial abstraction is the loss before any runoff starts: interception, infiltration and surface storage.

ideas.title: Rational formula
ideas.text: The rational method estimates peak runoff from a small catchment as Q = C i A. With intensity in in/h and area in acres, Q comes out in cfs with no conversion factor (the factor is 1.008). The intensity is the one for a storm lasting the time of concentration.

ideas.title: NRCS
ideas.text: The NRCS curve number method converts rainfall to runoff depth. The potential retention is S = 1,000/CN - 10 (inches), the initial abstraction is taken as 0.2 S, and runoff is Q = (P - 0.2S)^{2} / (P + 0.8S) when P exceeds 0.2 S.

ideas.title: NRCS
ideas.text: For mixed land cover, use the area-weighted average curve number. Pavement is assigned 98 because surface pits hold a little water.

examples.problem: A 18 acre parking area has a runoff coefficient of 0.70. The design rainfall intensity is 2.8 in/h. Using the rational method, what is the peak runoff?
examples.idea: The rational method estimates peak runoff from a small catchment as Q = C i A. With intensity in in/h and area in acres, Q comes out in cfs with no conversion factor (the factor is 1.008). The intensity is the one for a storm lasting the time of concentration.

examples.problem: A watershed with a curve number of 75 receives 6.0 in of rain. Using the NRCS (SCS) method, what is the depth of runoff?
examples.idea: The NRCS curve number method converts rainfall to runoff depth. The potential retention is S = 1,000/CN - 10 (inches), the initial abstraction is taken as 0.2 S, and runoff is Q = (P - 0.2S)^{2} / (P + 0.8S) when P exceeds 0.2 S.

examples.problem: A catchment is 3.0 ha of pavement (curve number 98) and 9.0 ha of lawn (curve number 70). What is the composite curve number?
examples.idea: For mixed land cover, use the area-weighted average curve number. Pavement is assigned 98 because surface pits hold a little water.

sections.deep:
Hydrology follows water from rainfall to runoff. Part of the rain is lost to interception, storage in depressions and infiltration; the rest runs off. The rational method estimates the peak flow from a small catchment as Q = C i A, using the rainfall intensity for a storm lasting the time of concentration. The NRCS curve number method estimates the depth of runoff from a storm depth and a number that reflects soil and land cover.

A hydrograph shows flow against time. A unit hydrograph is the response to one unit of runoff and scales linearly, so storms of other sizes and durations are built by scaling and adding. Design storms are chosen by return period.
method: Decide what is wanted: a peak flow, a runoff depth or a hydrograph.
For the rational method, find the time of concentration, read the intensity for that duration and return period, and use an area-weighted C.
For the curve number method, compute S, then the runoff depth.
For a unit hydrograph, multiply its ordinates by the runoff depth, and lag and add for successive periods.
Keep units consistent: in/h and acres give cfs directly.

sections.title: Basic hydraulics
sections.body:
Open channels flow with a free surface, driven by gravity down the slope and resisted by friction on the bed and banks. Manning's equation gives the velocity from the roughness, the hydraulic radius (flow area divided by wetted perimeter) and the slope.

Specific energy is depth plus velocity head. Critical depth is the depth of least energy for a given flow. Flow shallower and faster than critical is supercritical; deeper and slower is subcritical. The Froude number tells which: below 1 is subcritical. A hydraulic jump is the abrupt change from supercritical to subcritical.
pitfalls: Including the free water surface in the wetted perimeter.
Using the USCS constant 1.49 with SI units.
Mixing units in Hazen-Williams. Check which units the handbook form expects for diameter and flow.
Converting psi to feet of water without the factor: multiply by 144 and divide by 62.4, about 2.31 ft per psi.

example.problem: A rectangular channel 2 m wide flows 0.5 m deep. Find its hydraulic radius.

figure.alt: A rectangular channel 3 m wide flowing 1 m deep.
figure.caption: A rectangular channel. Hydraulic radius = flow area / wetted perimeter.

ideas.title: The hydraulic jump
ideas.text: Fast, shallow (supercritical) flow changes abruptly to slow, deep (subcritical) flow, as in the ring around the stream from a tap in a sink. The depth after the jump follows from the depth and Froude number before it: y_{2} = (y_{1} / 2)(\sqrt{1 + 8 Fr_{1}^{2}} - 1). The upstream Froude number must be greater than 1, which is a useful check on the arithmetic.

ideas.title: Weirs
ideas.text: Flow over a rectangular weir varies with the head to the 3/2 power: Q = C L H^{3/2}. A contracted weir, narrower than its channel, loses an effective 0.1 H of crest length for each end contraction.

ideas.title: Which friction formula
ideas.text: A Hazen-Williams C in the problem means the Hazen-Williams equation. A friction factor f or a Moody diagram means Darcy-Weisbach.

ideas.title: Manning's equation
ideas.text: Manning's equation for uniform open channel flow (SI): Q = (1/n) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}. The hydraulic radius R is the flow area divided by the wetted perimeter, which counts only the bed and sides in contact with water.

ideas.title: Critical depth
ideas.text: Critical depth is the depth of minimum specific energy for a given flow, where the Froude number equals 1. For a rectangular channel y_{c} = (q^{2} / g)^{1/3}, with q the flow per unit width. The minimum specific energy is 1.5 y_{c}.

ideas.title: Froude number
ideas.text: The Froude number compares the flow velocity with the speed of a small surface wave, the square root of g times the depth. Below 1 the flow is subcritical: deep, slow and controlled from downstream. Above 1 it is supercritical: shallow, fast and controlled from upstream. At exactly 1 it is critical.

ideas.title: Hydraulic jump
ideas.text: A hydraulic jump takes supercritical flow to subcritical. The depths on either side are conjugate: y_{2} = (y_{1} / 2)(square root of (1 + 8 Fr_{1}^{2}) - 1), with the Froude number taken upstream. It must exceed 1 for a jump to occur.

ideas.title: Weir
ideas.text: Flow over a sharp-crested rectangular weir varies with the head to the 3/2 power, so a small error in head matters. A suppressed weir spans the full channel width and has no end contractions.

examples.problem: A rectangular concrete channel is 3.5 m wide and flows 1.2 m deep on a slope of 0.0012. Manning's n is 0.014. What is the discharge?
examples.idea: Manning's equation for uniform open channel flow (SI): Q = (1/n) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}. The hydraulic radius R is the flow area divided by the wetted perimeter, which counts only the bed and sides in contact with water.

examples.problem: A rectangular channel carries a flow of 2.5 m^{3}/s per metre of width. What is the critical depth? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: Critical depth is the depth of minimum specific energy for a given flow, where the Froude number equals 1. For a rectangular channel y_{c} = (q^{2} / g)^{1/3}, with q the flow per unit width. The minimum specific energy is 1.5 y_{c}.

examples.problem: Water flows at 1.8 m/s and 1.20 m deep in a wide rectangular channel. What is the Froude number? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: The Froude number compares the flow velocity with the speed of a small surface wave, the square root of g times the depth. Below 1 the flow is subcritical: deep, slow and controlled from downstream. Above 1 it is supercritical: shallow, fast and controlled from upstream. At exactly 1 it is critical.
examples.steps:
Fr = \frac{V}{\sqrt{g y}} = \frac{1.8}{\sqrt{9.81(1.20)}} = \frac{1.8}{3.431} = 0.525.

This is less than 1, so the flow is subcritical.

examples.problem: Water flows 0.35 m deep at 6.5 m/s in a rectangular channel just before a hydraulic jump. What is the depth after the jump? Use g = 9.81 m/s^{2}.
examples.idea: A hydraulic jump takes supercritical flow to subcritical. The depths on either side are conjugate: y_{2} = (y_{1} / 2)(square root of (1 + 8 Fr_{1}^{2}) - 1), with the Froude number taken upstream. It must exceed 1 for a jump to occur.

examples.problem: A suppressed rectangular weir is 2.5 m long, and the head over its crest is 0.35 m. Using Q = 1.84 L H^{3/2} in SI units, what is the discharge?
examples.idea: Flow over a sharp-crested rectangular weir varies with the head to the 3/2 power, so a small error in head matters. A suppressed weir spans the full channel width and has no end contractions.

sections.deep:
Open channel flow has a free surface and is driven by gravity. In uniform flow the depth is constant and Manning's equation relates velocity to the hydraulic radius, slope and roughness. Specific energy, depth plus velocity head, is smallest at critical depth, where the Froude number is 1. Flow shallower and faster than critical is supercritical; deeper and slower is subcritical.

A hydraulic jump is the abrupt change from supercritical to subcritical flow, with a loss of energy. Pressure pipe flow uses the energy equation with Darcy-Weisbach or Hazen-Williams friction losses.
method: Compute the flow area and wetted perimeter, then the hydraulic radius.
Apply Manning's equation, with the 1.486 factor in U.S. units.
For flow regime, compute the Froude number or compare depth with critical depth.
For a jump, use the conjugate depth equation.
For pipes, write the energy equation with the friction loss.

sections.title: Pumps
sections.body:
A pump adds energy to water, measured as head: the height it could lift the water. The power delivered to the water is specific weight times flow times head. The motor must supply more than that because no pump is perfectly efficient.

A pump curve shows the head a pump produces at each flow. The system curve shows the head the piping needs. They cross at the operating point. The affinity laws predict the effect of changing speed: flow changes in proportion, head with the square and power with the cube. Too little pressure at the inlet causes cavitation, so the available net positive suction head must exceed what the pump requires.
pitfalls: Multiplying by efficiency instead of dividing when finding input power.

example.problem: A pump lifts 0.02 m^{3}/s through 25 m at 80% efficiency. Find the input power.

ideas.title: Pump power equation
ideas.text: The power added to the water is (specific weight) × Q × H. The pump must be supplied more than that because of its losses: brake power = water power / efficiency.

ideas.title: Affinity laws
ideas.text: The pump affinity laws relate performance at two speeds for the same impeller: flow varies with speed, head with speed squared and power with speed cubed.

examples.problem: A pump delivers 0.10 m^{3}/s of water against a total head of 36 m. The pump is 78% efficient. What power must be supplied to the pump?  Use 9.81 kN/m^{3}.
examples.idea: The power added to the water is (specific weight) × Q × H. The pump must be supplied more than that because of its losses: brake power = water power / efficiency.
examples.steps:
Water power = 9.81 × 0.10 × 36 = 35.32 kW.

Brake power = \frac{35.32}{0.78} = 45.3 kW.

examples.problem: A pump delivers 150 L/s at 1,150 rpm. Using the affinity laws, what flow does it deliver at 1,750 rpm?
examples.idea: The pump affinity laws relate performance at two speeds for the same impeller: flow varies with speed, head with speed squared and power with speed cubed.

sections.deep:
A pump adds energy to water, measured as head. The total dynamic head it must supply is the static lift plus friction and minor losses plus any pressure difference. Water power is specific weight × flow × head; the shaft must supply that divided by the pump efficiency.

The pump curve shows the head a pump delivers at each flow, and the system curve shows the head the piping needs. They cross at the operating point. Pumps in series add heads at the same flow; pumps in parallel add flows at the same head. The affinity laws scale flow, head and power with speed. Net positive suction head available must exceed that required, or the pump cavitates.
method: Compute the total dynamic head from the energy equation between the two reservoirs.
Compute water power, then divide by efficiency for shaft power.
For two pumps, build the combined curve: add heads (series) or flows (parallel).
Find the operating point where pump and system curves meet.
For a speed change, apply the affinity laws.

sections.title: Water distribution systems
sections.body:
A distribution system delivers treated water at adequate pressure to every tap and hydrant. It is sized for demand that swings through the day and the year: average day, maximum day, peak hour, plus fire flow. Storage tanks even out the swings and keep pressure up by elevation.

Head loss in pipes is found with the Hazen-Williams or Darcy-Weisbach equations. Pipes in series carry the same flow and their head losses add. Pipes in parallel share the flow so that the head loss is the same in each. Static pressure comes from the height of the water surface above the point.
pitfalls: Adding flows for pipes in series, or head losses for pipes in parallel.

example.problem: A tank's water surface is 30 m above a tap. Find the static pressure at the tap.

figure.caption: With no flow, pressure anywhere in the system is the specific weight of water times the height of the tank surface above that point.

ideas.title: Hydrant flow tests
ideas.text: A flow test measures the static pressure, then the residual pressure at a nearby hydrant while another is flowing. The flow available at a target residual, commonly 20 psi, scales with the ratio of the pressure drops raised to the 0.54 power.
Average day demand is population × per capita use. Treatment plants and sources are sized for the maximum day, found by applying a peaking factor to the average.

ideas.title: Pressure field in a static liquid
ideas.text: With no flow there are no friction losses, so the pressure anywhere in the system is hydrostatic: specific weight × the height of the water surface above that point.

examples.problem: A town of 60,000 people uses an average of 380 L per person per day. The maximum-day peaking factor is 1.7. What is the maximum-day demand?
examples.idea: Average day demand is population × per capita use. Treatment plants and sources are sized for the maximum day, found by applying a peaking factor to the average.

examples.problem: The water surface in an elevated tank is 46 m above a hydrant. With no flow in the system, what is the pressure at the hydrant? Use 9.81 kN/m^{3}.
examples.idea: With no flow there are no friction losses, so the pressure anywhere in the system is hydrostatic: specific weight × the height of the water surface above that point.

sections.deep:
A distribution system delivers water at adequate pressure for peak and fire demands. Demand varies through the day, so average, maximum-day and peak-hour demands are related by peaking factors, and storage evens out the difference between supply and use.

In a network, flow splits between parallel pipes so that the head loss is the same along each path, and flow is conserved at every junction. The hydraulic grade line shows pressure head plus elevation along the system; pressure at any point is the height of the grade line above the pipe times the specific weight.
method: Compute demands from population, per capita use and peaking factors.
For static pressure, multiply the specific weight by the height of the water surface above the point.
With flow, subtract the friction losses from the available head.
For parallel pipes, set head losses equal and flows adding to the total.
Size storage for equalising, fire and emergency volumes.

sections.title: Flood control
sections.body:
Floods are described by how often they are expected. A 100-year flood has a 1 in 100 chance of being equalled or exceeded in any year. It can happen two years running. Over a project's life, the chance of at least one such flood is far larger than the yearly chance.

Dams and reservoirs store flood water and release it slowly. Routing tracks a flood wave through a reservoir or river reach using inflow minus outflow equals change in storage. Spillways pass floods safely around a dam, and levees and floodways confine or divert the flow.

formulas.name: Storage routing
formulas.expr: inflow - outflow = change in storage per unit time

pitfalls: Reading a 100-year flood as one that comes exactly once a century.

example.problem: What is the chance of at least one 100-year flood during a 30-year mortgage?

ideas.title: Emergency spillways
ideas.text: An earth dam that is overtopped erodes and can fail. The emergency spillway carries flows beyond what the principal spillway can pass, so the water never reaches the crest.
A T-year event has probability 1/T in any one year. The chance that it does not occur in n independent years is (1 - 1/T)^{n}, so the risk of at least one occurrence is 1 - (1 - 1/T)^{n}.
The return period is the average interval between events of a given size or larger. Its reciprocal is the probability of that event being equalled or exceeded in any single year.

ideas.title: Forces on submerged surfaces
ideas.text: Check a one-metre length of dam as a rigid block. The water thrust is the area of the triangular pressure diagram, half the unit weight of water times the depth squared. Friction can supply up to the coefficient times the dam's weight.

examples.problem: What is the probability that a 100-year flood is equalled or exceeded at least once in a 50-year period?
examples.idea: A T-year event has probability 1/T in any one year. The chance that it does not occur in n independent years is (1 - 1/T)^{n}, so the risk of at least one occurrence is 1 - (1 - 1/T)^{n}.

examples.problem: What is the annual exceedance probability of a 500-year flood?
examples.idea: The return period is the average interval between events of a given size or larger. Its reciprocal is the probability of that event being equalled or exceeded in any single year.

examples.problem: A concrete gravity dam with a rectangular section is 5 m wide at the base and 7 m high. Water stands level with its top on one side. Concrete weighs 23.5 kN/m^{3}, the coefficient of friction on the base is 0.60 and uplift is ignored. What is the factor of safety against sliding?
examples.idea: Check a one-metre length of dam as a rigid block. The water thrust is the area of the triangular pressure diagram, half the unit weight of water times the depth squared. Friction can supply up to the coefficient times the dam's weight.

sections.deep:
Flood control starts with frequency. A T-year flood has a probability of 1/T of being equalled or exceeded in any one year, and the chance of at least one occurrence in n years is 1 - (1 - 1/T)^{n}. Design levels for structures follow from the acceptable risk over their life.

Control measures either store water (reservoirs and detention basins, which lower and delay the peak), convey it (channels and levees) or keep people out of its way (floodplain management). Routing a flood through storage uses the continuity equation: inflow minus outflow equals the change in storage.
method: Convert the return period to annual probability.
For risk over a period, compute 1 minus the probability of no exceedance.
For storage, apply inflow minus outflow times the time step.
Compare the reduced peak outflow with the capacity downstream.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.

sections.title: Stormwater
sections.body:
Development replaces soil and plants with roofs and pavement, so more rain runs off and it arrives faster. Stormwater design limits the damage. Detention basins hold runoff and release it slowly, cutting the peak. Retention basins hold it until it soaks in or evaporates.

Basin sizing is a bookkeeping exercise: storage rises when inflow exceeds outflow. Water quality practices such as swales, filters and settling capture the first flush, which carries most of the pollutants.
pitfalls: Forgetting to convert minutes to seconds.

example.problem: A basin receives 2.5 m^{3}/s and releases 0.5 m^{3}/s for 15 minutes. Find the volume stored.

ideas.title: Quality control and quantity control
ideas.text: Stormwater rules have two aims. Quality criteria treat the frequent small storms, for example a water quality volume or a target removal of suspended solids. Quantity criteria hold peak flows from large, rare storms to pre-development rates.
Storage routing is a volume balance: the change in storage equals inflow minus outflow, multiplied by the time step. Convert the time to seconds to match flows in m^{3}/s.

ideas.title: Rational formula
ideas.text: In Q = C i A, peak flow is directly proportional to the runoff coefficient when intensity and area are unchanged. The ratio of the coefficients is the ratio of the peak flows.

examples.problem: Stormwater flows into a detention basin at 4.2 m^{3}/s and leaves at 1.6 m^{3}/s for 25 minutes. How much water is stored in the basin during that time?
examples.idea: Storage routing is a volume balance: the change in storage equals inflow minus outflow, multiplied by the time step. Convert the time to seconds to match flows in m^{3}/s.
examples.steps: Change in storage = (inflow - outflow) × time = (4.2 - 1.6) × (25 × 60) = 2.6 × 1,500 = 3,900 m^{3}.

examples.problem: Development raises a site's runoff coefficient from 0.35 to 0.75. With the same rainfall intensity and area, by what factor does the rational-method peak flow increase?
examples.idea: In Q = C i A, peak flow is directly proportional to the runoff coefficient when intensity and area are unchanged. The ratio of the coefficients is the ratio of the peak flows.

sections.deep:
Stormwater design keeps runoff from development from damaging what lies downstream. Paving raises the runoff coefficient and shortens the time of concentration, so peaks rise sharply. Collection systems, the inlets, gutters and storm sewers, are sized for the peak flow from the rational method.

Detention basins hold the difference between the developed and pre-development hydrographs and release it at a controlled rate through an outlet such as an orifice or weir. Retention basins and infiltration practices also treat water quality.
method: Compute pre- and post-development peak flows.
Size pipes with Manning's equation for the design flow.
Estimate the required detention volume from the difference between inflow and allowed outflow over the storm.
Size the outlet with the orifice or weir equation for the allowed release.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.

sections.title: Collection systems
sections.body:
Sewers carry wastewater and stormwater by gravity in pipes that usually flow partly full. They are designed like open channels with Manning's equation. The slope must give enough velocity to keep solids moving, typically at least 0.6 m/s (2 ft/s) when flowing full.

Design flow is the average flow times a peaking factor, plus an allowance for groundwater and rain leaking in (infiltration and inflow). For a circular pipe flowing full, the hydraulic radius is a quarter of the diameter.
pitfalls: Using the diameter as the hydraulic radius.

example.problem: A sewer serves 5,000 people at 250 L per person per day with a peaking factor of 3.5. Find the peak flow in L/s.

ideas.title: Minimum slope for self-cleansing
ideas.text: Set the Manning velocity equal to the minimum, 0.6 m/s (2 ft/s), with the hydraulic radius D / 4, and solve for the slope. A circular pipe has the same hydraulic radius flowing full or half full.

ideas.title: Manning's equation
ideas.text: Manning's equation for velocity (SI): V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}. For a circular pipe flowing full the hydraulic radius is D / 4.
Sewers are sized for peak flow, the average flow multiplied by a peaking factor that is larger for small populations. Convert daily volume to L/s by dividing by 86,400 s per day.

ideas.title: Manning's equation
ideas.text: Set Manning's velocity equal to the self-cleansing minimum and solve for slope: S = (V n / R^{2/3})^{2}, with R = D / 4 for a full circular pipe. Larger pipes need flatter minimum slopes.

examples.problem: A 375 mm diameter sewer flows full on a slope of 0.004 with Manning's n = 0.013. What is the flow velocity?
examples.idea: Manning's equation for velocity (SI): V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}. For a circular pipe flowing full the hydraulic radius is D / 4.

examples.problem: A sewer serves 20,000 people who each generate 320 L of wastewater per day. With a peaking factor of 2.8, what is the peak flow?
examples.idea: Sewers are sized for peak flow, the average flow multiplied by a peaking factor that is larger for small populations. Convert daily volume to L/s by dividing by 86,400 s per day.

examples.problem: A 375 mm sewer flowing full must keep a velocity of at least 0.6 m/s. With Manning's n = 0.013, what minimum slope is needed, as a percentage?
examples.idea: Set Manning's velocity equal to the self-cleansing minimum and solve for slope: S = (V n / R^{2/3})^{2}, with R = D / 4 for a full circular pipe. Larger pipes need flatter minimum slopes.

sections.deep:
Wastewater collection systems are mostly gravity sewers flowing partly full. They are sized for peak flow, the average flow times a peaking factor, plus infiltration and inflow, and are laid at slopes that keep velocity high enough to move solids, commonly at least 0.6 m/s (2 ft/s).

Manning's equation governs. A circular pipe carries its greatest flow at about 93% of full depth, and its velocity when half full equals that when full. Lift stations and force mains are used where gravity flow is not possible.
method: Compute average flow from population and per capita flow, then apply the peaking factor.
Choose a diameter and slope and compute full-pipe capacity with Manning's equation.
Check that capacity exceeds the peak flow.
Check the self-cleansing velocity at low flow.
Use partial-flow relations if depth or velocity at a given flow is asked.

sections.title: Groundwater
sections.body:
Groundwater fills the gaps between soil grains below the water table. An aquifer is a layer that holds and passes useful amounts of water. Darcy's law says flow is proportional to the hydraulic conductivity of the soil and the slope of the water table (the hydraulic gradient).

The Darcy velocity is the flow per unit of total cross-section. The water itself moves faster because it only travels through the pores: divide by porosity for the seepage velocity. Pumping a well draws the water table down into a cone of depression.
pitfalls: Confusing Darcy velocity with seepage velocity.
In the unconfined well equation, using the drawdown as h. The h terms are the saturated thickness at each observation well: the original thickness minus the drawdown there.

example.problem: An aquifer has K = 20 m/day. Heads at two wells 500 m apart differ by 2 m. Find the Darcy velocity.

ideas.title: Darcy's law
ideas.text: Darcy's law for groundwater: Q = K i A. The hydraulic gradient i is the drop in head per unit distance along the flow path and has no units.

ideas.title: Darcy's law
ideas.text: Darcy velocity, K i, is flow per unit of total cross-section. Water only moves through the pores, so the actual average (seepage) velocity is larger: v = K i / n. Use seepage velocity for travel times of contaminants.

ideas.title: Dupuit
ideas.text: For steady flow to a well in an unconfined aquifer, Q = π K (h_{2}^{2} - h_{1}^{2}) / ln(r_{2} / r_{1}), where each h is the saturated thickness at that radius. Rearrange for K.

examples.problem: An aquifer has a hydraulic conductivity of 20 m/day and a hydraulic gradient of 0.006. What is the flow through a cross-section of 1,200 m^{2}?
examples.idea: Darcy's law for groundwater: Q = K i A. The hydraulic gradient i is the drop in head per unit distance along the flow path and has no units.

examples.problem: Groundwater moves through an aquifer with a hydraulic conductivity of 30 m/day, a hydraulic gradient of 0.005 and a porosity of 0.25. What is the average seepage velocity?
examples.idea: Darcy velocity, K i, is flow per unit of total cross-section. Water only moves through the pores, so the actual average (seepage) velocity is larger: v = K i / n. Use seepage velocity for travel times of contaminants.
examples.steps:
Darcy velocity = 30 × 0.005 = 0.15 m/day.

Seepage velocity = \frac{0.15}{0.25} = 0.6 m/day.

examples.problem: A well in an unconfined aquifer is pumped at 800 m^{3}/day. At steady state the saturated thickness is 20.0 m at 12 m from the well and 21.4 m at 60 m. What is the hydraulic conductivity?
examples.idea: For steady flow to a well in an unconfined aquifer, Q = π K (h_{2}^{2} - h_{1}^{2}) / ln(r_{2} / r_{1}), where each h is the saturated thickness at that radius. Rearrange for K.

sections.deep:
Groundwater moves through the pores of soil and rock under a hydraulic gradient, following Darcy's law, Q = K i A. An unconfined aquifer has a water table free to rise and fall; a confined aquifer is under pressure between less permeable layers.

Darcy velocity is flow over the total area; the actual seepage velocity is higher, Darcy velocity divided by effective porosity, because water moves only through the pores. Pumping a well draws down the water surface around it in a cone, and the steady-state well equations relate the pumping rate to drawdowns at two radii.
method: Compute the hydraulic gradient: head difference over flow length.
Apply Darcy's law for flow.
Divide by porosity for travel velocity and time.
For a well, choose the confined or unconfined equation and use two observation points.
Transmissivity is hydraulic conductivity times the saturated thickness.

sections.title: Water quality
sections.body:
Water quality is described by what is dissolved or suspended in the water. Dissolved oxygen keeps streams alive. Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) is the oxygen that bacteria use up while breaking down organic waste: high BOD starves a stream of oxygen.

Hardness is mainly calcium and magnesium and is reported as an equivalent amount of calcium carbonate. Alkalinity is the water's capacity to neutralize acid. pH measures acidity. Turbidity measures cloudiness. Concentrations convert to equivalents by dividing by the equivalent weight.
pitfalls: Forgetting to divide by the dilution fraction.

example.problem: A 10 mL sample diluted to 300 mL loses 4.0 mg/L of dissolved oxygen in five days. Find the BOD_{5}.

ideas.title: Eutrophication
ideas.text: Nutrients, mainly nitrogen and phosphorus, feed algal growth. When the algae die and decay, oxygen is consumed. Low dissolved oxygen is the symptom; a high level is not.

ideas.title: BOD
ideas.text: BOD is the oxygen consumed by microorganisms while they break down organic matter. In a diluted test, the drop in dissolved oxygen is divided by the fraction of the bottle that is sample: BOD = (DO_{initial} - DO_{final}) / P, with P = sample volume / bottle volume.

ideas.title: Hardness
ideas.text: Hardness is the sum of the multivalent cations, mainly calcium and magnesium, each converted to its CaCO_{3} equivalent: concentration × (50 / equivalent weight of the ion).

ideas.title: BOD
ideas.text: BOD is exerted as a first-order reaction: the oxygen used by time t is the ultimate BOD times (1 - e^{-k t}). A five-day test captures only part of the total, so the ultimate value is the five-day value divided by that fraction. Check whether k is given to base e or base 10.

examples.problem: A 8 mL wastewater sample is diluted to 300 mL in a BOD bottle. The dissolved oxygen falls from 8.4 mg/L to 3.2 mg/L in five days. What is the BOD_{5}?
examples.idea: BOD is the oxygen consumed by microorganisms while they break down organic matter. In a diluted test, the drop in dissolved oxygen is divided by the fraction of the bottle that is sample: BOD = (DO_{initial} - DO_{final}) / P, with P = sample volume / bottle volume.

examples.problem: A water sample contains 70 mg/L of calcium and 20 mg/L of magnesium. What is the total hardness, expressed as mg/L of CaCO_{3}? Use equivalent weights of 20 for calcium, 12.2 for magnesium and 50 for CaCO_{3}.
examples.idea: Hardness is the sum of the multivalent cations, mainly calcium and magnesium, each converted to its CaCO_{3} equivalent: concentration × (50 / equivalent weight of the ion).
examples.steps:
Calcium: 70 × \frac{50}{20} = 175.0 mg/L as CaCO_{3}.

Magnesium: 20 × \frac{50}{12.2} = 82.0 mg/L as CaCO_{3}.

Total hardness = 175.0 + 82.0 = 257.0 mg/L as CaCO_{3}.

examples.problem: A wastewater has a 5-day BOD of 200 mg/L and a BOD rate constant of 0.25 per day (base e). What is its ultimate BOD?
examples.idea: BOD is exerted as a first-order reaction: the oxygen used by time t is the ultimate BOD times (1 - e^{-k t}). A five-day test captures only part of the total, so the ultimate value is the five-day value divided by that fraction. Check whether k is given to base e or base 10.

sections.deep:
Water quality is described by what is dissolved or suspended in the water. Dissolved oxygen supports aquatic life and is used up as microorganisms break down organic matter, which is what BOD measures. BOD is exerted as a first-order reaction, approaching an ultimate value. Oxygen in a stream below a discharge falls and then recovers, the oxygen sag.

Concentrations are stated in mg/L, and mass loadings follow from flow times concentration. When two streams mix, the combined concentration is the flow-weighted average. Hardness and alkalinity are expressed as CaCO_{3} equivalents using equivalent weights.
method: For mixing, compute (Q_{1}C_{1} + Q_{2}C_{2}) / (Q_{1} + Q_{2}).
For BOD at time t, use the first-order expression with the rate constant given.
For a diluted BOD test, divide the oxygen drop by the sample fraction.
For mass loading, multiply flow by concentration and convert units.
Convert ions to CaCO_{3} equivalents by multiplying by 50 over the ion's equivalent weight.

sections.title: Testing and standards
sections.body:
Standards set the limits that water, wastewater, air and noise must meet, and standard tests check compliance. For drinking water, the maximum contaminant level (MCL) is the enforceable limit and the MCLG is the health goal. Wastewater discharges are limited by permit for BOD, suspended solids and other measures.

Air quality standards limit pollutants such as particulates and ozone. Noise is measured in decibels, a logarithmic scale: two equal sources together are 3 dB louder than one, and ten are 10 dB louder.

example.problem: Three identical machines each produce 70 dB. Find the combined level.

ideas.title: NPDES
ideas.text: The National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, under the Clean Water Act, regulates discharges from point sources such as treatment plant outfalls through permits.

ideas.title: Drinking water standards
ideas.text: Under the Safe Drinking Water Act a maximum contaminant level (MCL) is the enforceable limit. The maximum contaminant level goal is a health target that is not enforceable. Primary standards protect health; secondary standards cover taste, odour and appearance.

ideas.title: Wastewater standards
ideas.text: Discharges to surface water need a permit under the Clean Water Act's National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System. Secondary treatment is commonly defined as 30 mg/L of BOD_{5} and 30 mg/L of total suspended solids as 30-day averages, with at least 85% removal.

ideas.title: Routine tests
ideas.text: Turbidity measures clarity. Total coliform bacteria are used as indicator organisms for contamination. Other routine measures are pH, alkalinity, hardness, chlorine residual, dissolved oxygen, BOD and total suspended solids.

ideas.title: Sampling
ideas.text: A grab sample shows conditions at one moment. A composite sample combines portions collected over time and represents the average.

ideas.title: Sound pressure level
ideas.text: Decibels are logarithmic, so sound levels cannot be added directly. For n equal sources the combined level is L + 10 log_{10}(n): two equal sources add 3 dB, ten add 10 dB.

examples.problem: Five machines each produce a sound level of 85 dB at a receiver. What is the combined sound level when all of them run?
examples.idea: Decibels are logarithmic, so sound levels cannot be added directly. For n equal sources the combined level is L + 10 log_{10}(n): two equal sources add 3 dB, ten add 10 dB.

sections.deep:
Testing and standards tie water quality to law. Drinking water must meet maximum contaminant levels; wastewater discharges must meet permit limits. Each parameter has a standard test, and results are compared with the limit as an average or a maximum over a stated period.

Sampling matters as much as analysis: where, when and how the sample is taken decides what it represents. Indicator organisms stand in for pathogens because they are easier to detect.
method: Identify the parameter and the standard that governs it.
Decide whether the limit is enforceable or a goal.
Compute removal efficiency as (in - out) / in when a percentage is required.
Compare the result with the limit on the same averaging basis.

sections.title: Water and wastewater treatment
sections.body:
Drinking water treatment removes particles and kills germs. Coagulation and flocculation make fine particles clump, sedimentation lets the clumps settle, filtration strains out the rest, and disinfection kills what remains. Softening removes hardness.

Wastewater treatment removes solids and organic matter. Primary treatment settles solids. Secondary treatment uses bacteria, as in activated sludge, to consume dissolved organic matter. Tanks are sized by detention time (volume over flow) and by surface overflow rate (flow over surface area). Chemical feed is dose times flow.
pitfalls: Leaving detention time in days when hours are asked.
A dose of 1 mg/L equals 1 g/m^{3}, or 1 kg per 1,000 m^{3}.

example.problem: A 600 m^{3} tank treats 4,800 m^{3}/day. Find the detention time in hours.

ideas.title: Chemical dose from the reaction
ideas.text: For softening, write the reaction, convert the hardness to be removed into moles, apply the mole ratio and the chemical's molecular weight, then divide by its purity.

ideas.title: Hydraulic residence time
ideas.text: Hydraulic detention time is the average time water spends in a tank: volume divided by flow rate. Watch the time units; a flow in m^{3}/day gives a time in days.

ideas.title: Overflow rate
ideas.text: The surface overflow rate, Q / A, is the upward velocity of water in a clarifier. A particle is removed if its settling velocity is at least the overflow rate, so the rate is the key design parameter and depth does not appear.
Mass feed rate = flow × concentration. A dose of 1 mg/L is 1 g/m^{3}, so m^{3}/day × mg/L gives g/day; divide by 1,000 for kg/day.

examples.problem: A sedimentation tank has a volume of 2,700 m^{3} and treats a flow of 14,400 m^{3}/day. What is the detention time?
examples.idea: Hydraulic detention time is the average time water spends in a tank: volume divided by flow rate. Watch the time units; a flow in m^{3}/day gives a time in days.

examples.problem: A clarifier treats 15,000 m^{3}/day and has a surface area of 420 m^{2}. What is its surface overflow rate?
examples.idea: The surface overflow rate, Q / A, is the upward velocity of water in a clarifier. A particle is removed if its settling velocity is at least the overflow rate, so the rate is the key design parameter and depth does not appear.

examples.problem: A plant treats 36,000 m^{3}/day and applies a chlorine dose of 2.5 mg/L. How much chlorine is used per day?
examples.idea: Mass feed rate = flow × concentration. A dose of 1 mg/L is 1 g/m^{3}, so m^{3}/day × mg/L gives g/day; divide by 1,000 for kg/day.

sections.deep:
Treatment is a chain of unit processes, each removing a class of contaminants. Conventional drinking water treatment is coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration and disinfection. Wastewater treatment is preliminary screening and grit removal, primary settling, biological secondary treatment such as activated sludge, secondary settling and disinfection.

Tanks are sized by a few simple ratios: detention time is volume over flow, overflow rate is flow over surface area and weir loading is flow over weir length. Chemical feed is flow times dose. Activated sludge adds the food-to-microorganism ratio and solids retention time. Disinfection is judged by concentration times contact time.
method: Identify the process and its design parameter.
Compute detention time as volume / flow in consistent time units.
Compute overflow rate as flow / surface area.
Compute chemical mass as flow × dose, with 1 mg/L equal to 1 g/m^{3} or 8.34 lb per million gallons.
Compare the result with typical design ranges if given.
